analysis.one_liner: Replaces the federal income tax with a flat 20% tax on wages and business income, and repeals the estate tax.
analysis.headline: Introduced by Sen. Arlen Specter with zero cosponsors in April 1999, the bill was sent to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a vote before the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would throw out the current income tax and replace it with a single 20% rate on two things: wages and salaries people earn from work, and business income. It keeps only a few deductions: a large standard deduction, cash charitable gifts up to $2,500, and home purchase loan interest. It would also repeal the estate and gift taxes, end the public financing fund for presidential campaigns, and end the dedicated fund that pays health benefits for retired coal miners. Notably, income from investments like stock sales, dividends, and interest would no longer be taxed at the individual level at all.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live mainly on investment income would pay no individual income tax, since the bill taxes only earned income like wages. Owners of the largest estates would no longer owe estate or gift taxes. Businesses would pay a flat 20% on profits after deducting wages, equipment, and supplies, and would no longer face separate corporate tax structures.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Investors, large estates, and business owners

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a single 20% rate on individual earned income and on business income, replacing the current multi-rate structure [S2][S3].

Allows a standard deduction of $17,500 for joint filers plus $5,000 per dependent, indexed to inflation, along with a $2,500 cash charitable deduction and a deduction for home acquisition loan interest [S3].
Allows businesses to deduct the cost of inputs, employee compensation, and the full cost of property used in the business, and to carry excess deductions into later years with interest [S3].
Repeals the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes for deaths and transfers after December 31, 1999 [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Wage earners, whose income is the only individual income the bill taxes, would bear the 20% rate while investment income goes untaxed. Low- and middle-income families would lose the child tax credit, earned income credit, and most itemized deductions. Retired coal miners would lose their federally funded health benefits, and the presidential campaign public financing fund would be abolished.
analysis.who_pays_short: Wage earners, retirees, and federal programs

drawbacks.text: The bill taxes only 'earned income' — wages, salaries, and professional fees — so capital gains, dividends, interest, and rents would face no individual income tax, shifting the overall tax burden toward people who work for a living [S3].

It repeals all current individual and business tax provisions and replaces them with a 20% flat tax, meaning families lose the child tax credit, earned income credit, and most itemized deductions, keeping only a standard deduction, a $2,500 cash charity deduction, and home purchase interest [S2][S3].
Repealing the estate and gift taxes eliminates the only federal tax on very large inherited fortunes [S2][S3].
It repeals the provisions financing retired coal miners' health benefits, ending a dedicated funding stream for those retirees [S2][S3].
It repeals the public financing of presidential elections, removing the voluntary checkoff that funds campaigns and reduces dependence on private donations [S2][S3].
The bill disallows business deductions for lobbying and political expenditures, but only by denying businesses a tax write-off for those costs — it does not restrict lobbying itself [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would simplify taxes dramatically — a postcard-size return with one rate and few deductions is a real benefit for filers. But the design taxes only wages at the individual level and untaxes investment income entirely, while repealing the estate tax, so the largest gains flow to households with the most wealth rather than to people who work for pay. Families who rely on the child tax credit or earned income credit, and retirees depending on the coal miners' health fund, would bear real losses. On balance, the costs fall on wage earners and specific vulnerable groups while the benefits concentrate at the top.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee on April 15, 1999, and the committee never acted on it, so it died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Sen. Arlen Specter introduced the Flat Tax Act of 1999 in the Senate on April 15, 1999 [S1][S5].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance, which took no further action [S5].
No vote was ever held in the Senate or House, and the bill expired with the end of the 106th Congress on January 3, 2001 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wage-earning taxpayers, retired coal miners, and the presidential public financing system are no worse off, because the bill never advanced; no group gained from its death, since it was a single-sponsor proposal that never gathered momentum.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo held; no group gained

for.name: Sen. Arlen Specter
for.role: U.S. Senator from Pennsylvania, sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 15, 1999 and delivered introductory remarks; it was referred to the Finance Committee [S1][S5].

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: The committee to which the bill was referred; it took no action for the rest of the Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on April 15, 1999 and never reported it out, held no markup, and the Senate never considered it [S5].

sides.party_line_note: A single Republican senator sponsored the bill with no cosponsors from either party, and no votes were ever taken, so the partisan shape of the chamber cannot be measured.

industries.industry: High-wealth households and heirs of large estates
industries.note: The bill taxes only earned income, leaving investment income untaxed at the individual level, and repeals the estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes entirely [S3]. The wealthiest households would pay dramatically less while wage earners bear the 20% rate.

All business activity would be taxed at a flat 20% after deducting inputs, wages, and full equipment costs, replacing the existing corporate tax structure with a lower, simpler levy [S3]. The cost of that revenue loss would fall on other taxpayers or federal programs.
The charitable deduction would shrink to cash gifts only, capped at $2,500, reducing the incentive for donors to give [S3]. Nonprofits that depend on large deductible donations would feel that loss.

industries.industry: Retired coal miners' health benefit fund
industries.note: The bill repeals the subtitle of the tax code that finances health benefits for retired coal miners and their dependents [S2][S3]. Those benefits would end unless funded another way.

Interest on loans to buy or build a home stays deductible, but home-equity borrowing beyond the acquisition limit loses its deduction, and the deduction no longer scales with income since rates flatten [S3].
